assumptions: That the deploy at 15:13 is the cause is an assumption, not a finding: it was never tested by a rollback and no evidence directly links the released code to the latency.

The change-event and feature-flag histories were assumed complete; the responder found one deploy and zero recent flag changes, and took that to mean no other change occurred. Infrastructure, database, and upstream-dependency changes were never queried at all.
Dependency and resource-level telemetry (downstream call latency, CPU/memory/connection-pool saturation) was never retrieved, so 'no dependency problem' was assumed rather than checked.
Recovery is assumed to have been spontaneous, since no mitigation was applied; whether the condition actually cleared or merely fell below alert thresholds was not verified.

The four minutes of per-minute metrics and the handful of log lines read (the same lines re-read on each of the three investigation passes) were treated as representative of the whole incident; no broader baseline was examined.
The draft pull request was proposed without a confirmed root cause, so it is assumed to address the real defect rather than verified to.
Impact was assumed to be limited to this one service; no check was made for correlated degradation in callers or sibling services.
input.executive_summary: For a short window on the afternoon of 16 September (the alert opened at 15:16 UTC and cleared at 15:19 UTC per the incident record), one shop service responded far more slowly than normal — response times climbed from roughly a fifth of a second to five-second timeouts over about three minutes — and a minority of customer requests failed during that window rather than completing. The service recovered on its own; no configuration was changed, nothing was rolled back, and no customer-facing workaround was applied, so the recovery was not the result of any action taken during the incident. The automated responder investigated three times, each time identifying a code release pushed minutes before the slowdown as the most likely cause, but it could not confirm this and had no safe, reversible action to apply. It therefore opened a draft code change for human review and escalated to an engineer. The cause is still unconfirmed and the same failure could recur; the open review item and a decision on whether to roll back that release are the outstanding follow-ups.
input.root_cause: Not established. io-shop p95 latency rose from a ~220ms baseline at 15:13 to 900ms, then 1800ms, then 5000ms timeouts by 15:16, and the only recorded production change to the service in the preceding weeks was the deploy of revision 9f4c1e7b2a3d5c8e1f0b6a4d2c9e7b5a3f1d8c6e at 15:13 — a one-minute temporal correlation that was never confirmed, because no rollback or other mitigation was performed and the logs name no code path, dependency, or saturated resource. A slow downstream dependency or resource exhaustion coincident with the deploy remains equally consistent with the evidence gathered.
